about.title: San Pablo Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Slip and fall incidents in San Pablo happen in ordinary places: grocery aisles near San Pablo Avenue, apartment stairwells off 23rd Street, or parking lots along Rumrill Boulevard. What turns a bad fall into a viable claim is proof — did the property owner know, or should they have known, about the wet floor, broken step, or uneven pavement, and did they fail to fix or warn about it? California law places that burden on the injured person, which is why documenting the hazard quickly matters so much. Surveillance footage from stores and apartment complexes is often overwritten within days or weeks, so time works against you. LawProactive doesn't practice law; we simply connect San Pablo residents hurt on someone else's property with an independent attorney who can start gathering evidence, request video preservation, and evaluate what happened. There's no cost to find out where you stand, and no obligation to move forward.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a San Pablo Premises Case

items.title: Notice Has to Be Shown
items.desc: California requires proof the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney can help track down maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that speak to that.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many San Pablo businesses and apartment complexes overwrite security footage within days. Getting a preservation request out early can be the difference between having evidence and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you can still pursue compensation — it's simply reduced by your share of fault, not eliminated.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in San Pablo?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity — a city building or transit stop, for example — the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim, so it's worth checking quickly.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the fall?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still recover compensation even if you share some blame, such as not seeing a posted warning sign. Any amount recovered would just be reduced by your percentage of fault. It's still worth having someone evaluate the specifics.

items.question: I fell at a business near San Pablo Avenue — what should I do first?
items.answer: If you're able, take photos of the hazard, note the time and any witnesses, and ask the business to preserve any security video before it's automatically deleted. Then consider getting connected with an attorney quickly, since evidence at busy corridor locations tends to disappear fast.
